```{r}
library(brms)       # Bayesian Regression Model
library(bayesplot)  # Diagnostics
library(loo)        # LOOCV Model comparison
library(tidyverse)  # Data manipulation
library(corrplot)   # Correlation Matrix Visualization
library(car)        # VIF
```

# Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r}
dat <- read.csv("data.csv")
dim(dat)[1]
```

```{r}
dat$Season <- factor(dat$Season)

# select the continuous variables
num <- dat %>% 
  select(PH, IFP, NLP, NGP, NGL, NS, MHG, GY)

# check the correlation matrix
cov <- cor(num)

corrplot(cov, 
         addCoef.col = "black",
         tl.col = "red",
         number.cex = 0.7)
```

```{r}
fit_vif <- lm(GY ~ Season + PH + IFP + NLP, data = dat)
vif(fit_vif)
```

We choose Season, PH, IFP, and NLP as the regressors.

# Fitting

```{r}
set.seed(123)

# BRM, using Markov Chain Monte Carlo Method
fit <- brm(GY ~  Season + PH + IFP + NLP, data = dat)

# interaction model
fit.2 <- brm(GY ~ Season * (PH + IFP + NLP), data = dat)
```

# Diagnostics

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

```{r}
summary(fit.2)
```

According to the outputs, all ESS values are larger than the standard diagnostic threshold of 1000, we can safely conclude that both models are reliable.
And since all parameters have $\hat{R}=1$, it implies that the independent MCMC chains have reached a perfect consensus and successfully converged, signaling that the sampling process is stable and the results are mathematically reliable.

# Model Selection

We use LOOCV to calculate the Expected Log-Pointwise Predictive Density (ELPD), which is the accuract score.

```{r}
set.seed(123)

# Using LOOCV to compare two models
loo.1 <- loo(fit)
loo.2 <- loo(fit.2)
loo_compare(loo.1, loo.2)
```

By checking the $Ratio = \frac{|elpd\_diff|}{se\_diff} = 1.95$ of fit, the accuracy of fit.2 significantly better than fit.

```{r}
# 95% CI for the coefficients
fixef(fit.2)
```

Since the CI of $\beta_{PH}$ and $\beta_{Season2:PH}$ include 0, indicating there is no significant effect at 0.05 level of significant, we need to refit a simpler model.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
fit.3 <- brm(GY ~ Season * (IFP + NLP), data = dat)
summary(fit.3)
```

```{r}
set.seed(123)
loo.3 <- loo(fit.3)
loo_compare(loo.2, loo.3)
```

```{r}
# 95% CI for the coefficients
fixef(fit.3)
```

Checking the outputs, we can say fit.3 is a better model than fit.2.

# Posterior Predictive Check

```{r}
pp_check(fit.3, ndraws = 100)
```

# Visualization

```{r}
mcmc_trace(fit.3, c("b_Season2", "b_IFP", "b_NLP", "b_Season2:IFP", "b_Season2:NLP"))
```

```{r}
# posterior distributions of the coefficients
mcmc_areas(fit.3, "b_Season2", prob = 0.95)
```

```{r}
mcmc_areas(fit.3, "b_IFP", prob = 0.95)
```

```{r}
mcmc_areas(fit.3, "b_NLP", prob = 0.95)
```

```{r}
mcmc_areas(fit.3, "b_Season2:IFP", prob = 0.95)
```

```{r}
mcmc_areas(fit.3, "b_Season2:NLP", prob = 0.95)
```

```{r}
bayes_R2(fit.3)
```

# Conclusion

We can conclude 

Our final model is:

In Season 1:
$$
\text{GY} = 1759.63 + 76.29(\text{IFP}) + 7.10(\text{NLP})
$$
In Season 2:
$$
\text{GY} = (1759.63 + 1549.42) + (76.29 - 80.87)\text{IFP} + (7.10 - 4.35)\text{NLP}
$$
$$
\text{GY} = 3309.05 - 4.58(\text{IFP}) + 2.75(\text{NLP})
$$

with SE(Residual) = 478.95.
